{{short description|Formula in classical differential geometry}}
{{other uses|Clairaut's formula (disambiguation)}}

In classical [[differential geometry]], '''Clairaut's relation''', named after [[Alexis Claude de Clairaut]], is a formula that characterizes the great circle paths on the [[unit sphere]].  The formula states that if <math> \gamma </math> is a parametrization of a great circle then 

:<math> \rho(\gamma(t)) \sin \psi(\gamma(t)) = \text{constant},\, </math>

where <math> \rho(P) </math> is the distance from a point <math> P </math> on the [[great circle]] to the <math> z </math>-axis, and <math> \psi(P) </math> is the angle between the great circle and the [[Meridian (geography)|meridian]] through the point <math> P </math>.

The relation remains valid for a [[geodesic]] on an arbitrary [[surface of revolution]].

A statement of the general version of Clairaut's relation is:<ref name=Pressley>{{cite book |author=Andrew Pressley |title=Elementary Differential Geometry |page=183 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UXPyquQaO6EC&dq=%22Clairaut%27s+theorem%22&pg=PA185 
|isbn=1-85233-152-6 |publisher=Springer |year=2001  }}</ref>
{{quotation|Let <math> \gamma </math> be a [[geodesic]] on a [[surface of revolution]] <math> S </math>, let <math> \rho </math> be the distance of a point of <math> S </math> from the [[axis of rotation]], and let <math> \psi </math> be the angle between <math> \gamma </math> and the [[Meridian (geography)|meridian]] of <math> S </math>. Then <math> \rho \sin \psi </math> is constant along <math> \gamma </math>. Conversely, if  <math> \rho \sin \psi </math> is constant along some curve <math> \gamma </math> in the surface, and if no part of <math> \gamma </math> is part of some parallel of <math> S </math>, then <math> \gamma </math> is a geodesic.|Andrew Pressley: ''Elementary Differential Geometry'', p. 183}}
Pressley (p.&nbsp;185) explains this theorem as an expression of [[conservation of angular momentum]] about the [[axis of revolution]] when a particle moves along a geodesic under no forces other than those that keep it on the surface.

Now imagine a particle constrained to move on a surface of revolution, without external torque around the axis. By conservation of angular momentum:
:<math> r \, v_\theta = L, </math>
where

* <math>r</math> = distance to the axis,
* <math>v_\theta</math> = component of velocity orthogonal to the meridian,
* <math>L</math> = conserved angular momentum around the axis.

But geometrically,
:<math>v_\theta = |v| \sin \psi, </math>

If we normalize so the speed <math>|v|=1</math> (unit speed geodesics), we get:
:<math>r \sin \psi = \frac{L}{|v|} = \text{constant}. </math>

==References==
*[[Manfredo do Carmo|M. do Carmo]], ''Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces'', page 257.
